chapter.title: The spark: from Munich to the invasion of Poland

cards.body: Picture the street in 1938. Smoke is already curling from one window of the German house, and the neighbours in Britain and France are standing on the pavement with their hoses coiled, saying: *let it burn out, he only wants that one room.* **Each time they waited, the fire took another room**, until on 1 September 1939 it jumped the fence into Poland.
cards.simpler: Imagine a street in 1938. Smoke is already coming from one window of the German house. The neighbours, Britain and France, stand on the pavement with their hoses still coiled up. They say: *let it burn out, he only wants that one room.* **Each time they waited, the fire took another room.** On 1 September 1939 it jumped the fence into Poland.

cards.prompt: It's 1938. A neighbour keeps knocking through walls into the empty houses next door, swearing each time that this is the last one. You are the street. What do you most likely do?

options.text: Call the fire brigade the first time, before anything spreads
Agree to the latest one if he promises, in writing, that it is the last
Knock through his wall first, to show you mean it

whyNot.a: That's what hindsight says, not what the street did: in 1938 nobody wanted another 1914, so the hoses stayed coiled.
whyNot.c: That's starting the fire yourself, not stopping it: Britain and France were desperate to avoid a war, not to begin one.

cards.reteach: Nobody on the street had forgotten the last war, which had killed millions and ended only 20 years earlier. So the neighbours chose the cheapest-looking option each time: give Hitler what he asked for and get a promise. That habit has a name, appeasement, and this chapter is about how it ran out.

cards.title: Three grabs, no shots fired
cards.body:
From 1936 to 1939 Hitler took land in steps, each one bigger than the last. In March 1936 he marched troops into the Rhineland, a strip of Germany along the French border that the 1919 treaty had said must stay free of soldiers. France protested and did nothing.

In March 1938 he took Austria whole. Then he demanded the Sudetenland, the German-speaking edge of Czechoslovakia.

**At each step the pattern held**: a grab, a loud complaint from Britain and France, then acceptance. Hitler learned the lesson fast. The street talked a lot and never picked up a hose.
cards.simpler:
From 1936 to 1939 Hitler took land in steps, each bigger than the last. In March 1936 he sent soldiers into the Rhineland, a strip of Germany beside France where the 1919 peace treaty banned troops. France complained and did nothing.

In March 1938 he took all of Austria. Then he demanded the Sudetenland, the German-speaking edge of Czechoslovakia.

**Each time the same thing happened**: a grab, loud complaints from Britain and France, then acceptance. Hitler learned fast.

cards.title: A piece of paper, September 1938
cards.body: On 30 September 1938 Britain's prime minister, Neville Chamberlain, flew home from a meeting with Hitler in Munich. He and France had agreed that Germany could have the Sudetenland. Czechoslovakia, the country losing the land, had not been invited to the table. Chamberlain stepped off the plane waving a signed note in which Hitler promised the two countries would never go to war again, and told the crowd it meant *peace for our time*. The note held for just under a year.
cards.simpler: On 30 September 1938 Britain's prime minister, Neville Chamberlain, flew home from a meeting with Hitler in Munich. He and France had agreed to let Germany have the Sudetenland. Czechoslovakia, the country losing the land, had not been invited. Chamberlain got off the plane waving a signed note. In it Hitler promised Britain and Germany would never go to war again. Chamberlain told the crowd it meant *peace for our time*. **The note held for just under a year.**

cards.prompt: A pub quiz asks: what did Britain and France actually decide at Munich in September 1938?

options.text: To let Germany take the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia in exchange for a promise of no more grabs
To declare war on Germany if it moved one step further
To split Poland between Germany and the Soviet Union

whyNot.b: That's the guarantee they gave Poland in 1939, not the Munich deal: at Munich they gave way, they did not threaten.
whyNot.c: That's the Hitler-Stalin pact of August 1939, not Munich: Britain and France were not part of that one.

cards.reteach: Munich is the clearest case of appeasement, which means giving way to avoid a fight. Britain and France handed over a piece of Czechoslovakia that was not theirs to give, and took a promise in return. The promise was the whole point for them, and it was worth nothing to Hitler.

cards.title: The promise breaks, then the shock
cards.body:
In March 1939 Hitler took the rest of Czechoslovakia. Nobody had been asked, and there were no German speakers to rescue this time. **The excuse that he only wanted Germans back was dead.** Britain and France finally promised to fight if Poland, his obvious next target, was attacked.

Then came the shock. On 23 August 1939 Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union, bitter enemies in public, signed a pact not to fight each other. A secret part of it carved Poland up between them.

With Stalin out of the way, Hitler attacked Poland on 1 September 1939. Britain and France declared war two days later, on 3 September.
cards.simpler:
In March 1939 Hitler took the rest of Czechoslovakia. Nobody was asked, and no German speakers lived there to rescue. **His excuse of bringing Germans home was dead.** Britain and France now promised to fight if he attacked Poland, his next target.

On 23 August 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union, enemies in public, agreed not to fight each other and secretly split Poland between them.

Hitler attacked Poland on 1 September. Britain and France declared war on 3 September.

cards.body: Sam, revising for a test, writes that Britain and France declared war because Germany invaded Czechoslovakia. It sounds right, because Czechoslovakia was the famous betrayal. But in March 1939 they protested and did nothing, again. The line they actually fought over was Poland, 6 months later. Spot the slip by asking: which country had the written guarantee? Only Poland did.
cards.simpler: Sam is revising for a test and writes that Britain and France declared war because Germany invaded Czechoslovakia. It sounds right, because Czechoslovakia was the famous betrayal. But when Hitler took it in March 1939, they complained and did nothing, again. **The country they actually went to war over was Poland**, six months later. To catch the slip, ask: which country had a written promise of help? Only Poland did.

cards.prompt: Four moments: Rhineland 1936, Austria 1938, the Sudetenland at Munich 1938, Poland 1939. What separates the last one from the first three?

options.text: Poland was the first grab with no German speakers to justify it
Poland was the first one Britain and France had promised in advance to fight for
Poland was the first time Hitler used soldiers rather than a vote

whyNot.a: That's the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939, not Poland: that grab killed the excuse, but the street still did not fight.
whyNot.c: That's not the dividing line: the Rhineland in 1936 was also done with marching troops, and nobody fought over it.

cards.reteach: Three grabs passed because each time the neighbours chose a promise over a fight. What changed in 1939 was not Hitler, who did what he always did, but the street: after Czechoslovakia vanished, Britain and France had pledged in writing to defend Poland. When the tanks crossed on 1 September, the promise finally cost something.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: From 1936 to 1938 Hitler grabbed the Rhineland, Austria and the Sudetenland, and Britain and France let each one pass to avoid another war, most famously at Munich. **When he swallowed the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939, then made a deal with Stalin and invaded Poland on 1 September, their patience was spent**, and they declared war on 3 September.
cards.simpler: Between 1936 and 1938 Hitler grabbed the Rhineland, Austria and the Sudetenland. Britain and France let each one go to avoid another war, most famously at the Munich meeting. **When he swallowed the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939, then made a deal with Stalin, the Soviet leader, and invaded Poland on 1 September, their patience ran out.** They declared war on 3 September.

cards.body: Tonight, say the chain aloud to someone in under a minute: Rhineland, Austria, Munich, rest of Czechoslovakia, Stalin pact, Poland, war. Six steps, then the match.
cards.simpler: Tonight, tell someone the chain of events out loud in under a minute: Rhineland, Austria, Munich, the rest of Czechoslovakia, the deal with Stalin, Poland, war. **Six steps, then the match is struck.** Saying it aloud is like walking a route once so you can find it again.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now list the steps from Munich to Britain and France declaring war on 3 September 1939, and say why they waited so long.
